name: Zane Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the West Yard flats, fixing battens and carrying door sets up from the loading bay. I am fifty-eight and still junior in this trade; I spent years as a caretaker before a neighbour helped me get on a site, and I left school early. My partner Priya works at the library, and our grown children have their own homes. The builder pays a good site rate and we have about ten months of expenses saved. I like the moment a door shuts without scraping, although I still need the lead carpenter to check my first cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little AI on purchase lists is all right if it is tested before anyone loses hours over it. I've tried a phone assistant a few times, but a wrong timber size still has to be fixed by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not expecting a wage shock from a small change. Priya's library work, our ten-month reserve and the other builders in town make this one manageable, even though I'm a junior worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting battens and door sets at West Yard. In the first year I'd ask lead carpenter Ivo to show me a completed AI purchase list, compare it with the delivery and then use the tool only if the counts match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this picture because I have time to check a tool properly. I would still raise a bad order at the site meeting rather than let the next crew repeat it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when you tried the phone assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gave me three types of screw when the job needed one, so I went back to Ivo's marked drawing. That cost a few minutes, not anyone's job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a bad order change how you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop using it for orders until the list was corrected and other workers could see what went wrong. My rule is simple: test it on a real delivery before trusting it.

say: I'd accept **AI purchase lists** once a real delivery confirms their counts.
I'd speak up if a **wrong timber size** costs the crew time.
think: I expect **stable wages** with a small software change.
Priya's library job and our **ten-month reserve** give us room to check tools carefully.
do: Keep fitting **battens and doors** at West Yard.
Compare an **AI purchase list** against the delivered materials before using it.
feel: **Calm** about small changes, with an eye on errors affecting the next crew.
S0.quote: My rule is simple: test it on a real delivery before trusting it.
fieldNote: Zane's caution comes from a **screw-list error**, yet he is willing to adopt a tool after a real delivery test.
His higher site pay, Priya's library work and a **ten-month reserve** support a calm response to modest change.

steps.text: Keep fitting door sets and battens at West Yard
Try the AI purchase list after comparing it with deliveries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site meeting that software may speed up buying, but workers should get training time and a say in the new schedule. I would ask the union steward to put any change to hours in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may do estimates with fewer people, and that could eventually thin our site bookings. My hands are still needed for doors, and there are many builders nearby, so I am more watchful than scared for my own wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll sit in on the next buying-tool demonstration and ask Ivo to let me compare a live list with the delivery docket. During the first year I'd keep my site shifts, and I'd take the steward a copy of the hours board if the firm quietly reduces the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because office changes can reach the loading bay in ways managers miss. I don't think Priya and I are about to lose our home, but I want a record before things slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the steward to seek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for notice of roster changes and paid time to learn any screen the firm requires. The people carrying the doors should not cover the cost of a manager's experiment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new buying tool on your own time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd practise once I saw it working on our job, preferably during a paid shift. I use AI sometimes, but I don't want a broken order blamed on an unpaid evening of guessing.

say: I'd seek **paid training time** for any required buying tool.
I'd ask the steward for **written roster changes**.
think: Fewer **office estimators** might reduce future site bookings.
Our savings and many **local builders** make my own wage risk manageable for now.
do: Watch a **live buying demonstration** and compare the delivery docket.
Keep **site shifts** and share reduced-hour records with the steward.
feel: **Uneasy** about delayed site effects, without expecting immediate household loss.
S1.quote: The people carrying the doors should not cover the cost of a manager's experiment.
fieldNote: Zane links new software to **paid learning** and written roster notice, using the steward for practical records.
He expects his physical work to continue in the near term and has several **local employers** as a fallback.

steps.text: Practise the buying tool on a live paid shift after it proves useful
Keep taking paid West Yard shifts
Bring reduced-hours records to the union steward if cuts appear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that full thinking AI in 2028 could change the drawings and buying before any robot enters West Yard. I would ask our union branch to negotiate safe work and proper notice before the 2031 machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty when the office work changes and sixty-three when a robot might fit doors. Our ten-month cushion gives me time, yet a broad cut to junior site roles could take away the higher wage Priya and I have used to build it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll put extra from full site months into savings and ask Ivo to show me the digital checks he trusts. In 2029 I'd keep paid door work while offered and attend the branch meeting about robot safety; if the rota falls, I'd apply to the local housing-maintenance crews rather than wait for savings to drain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real loss of site wages after 2031, even with money saved. Having other builders close by gives me something useful to do while the dates are still ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask of the maintenance crews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether they have paid vacancies and whether their work is mostly repair in occupied homes. I would not leave a well-paid site shift for a job notice with no wage listed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a robot assignment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a supervised trial and clear safety rules, and I would want the crew paid for that training. I am open to a proven machine, not to standing beside an untested one.

say: I'd name the gap between **2028 drawings** and 2031 site robots.
I'd ask the union for **safety and notice** before robots arrive.
think: At **sixty-three**, broad junior cuts could remove my higher site wage.
Our **ten-month reserve** buys search time, but cannot replace a lasting income.
do: Save extra from **full site months** and inspect trusted digital checks.
Keep **paid door work** in 2029 and attend the safety meeting.
Apply to **housing maintenance** if the rota falls.
feel: **Anxious** about possible site wage loss, while local vacancies offer options.
S2.quote: I am open to a proven machine, not to standing beside an untested one.
fieldNote: Zane's concern sharpens at the **hands-on robot date**, while he keeps the earlier office change distinct.
He will search before the **reserve drains** and insists any robot training be supervised, safe and paid.

steps.text: Add extra savings after full West Yard months
Keep taking paid door shifts in 2029
Attend the union branch meeting on robot safety
Apply to local housing-maintenance crews if site hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the workforce time to test equipment and bargain over its use. I want a record of faults and a real training schedule, not just a poster about innovation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three the thinking system may replace office tasks, and at sixty-six robots may do some door fitting. Priya and I may choose fewer shifts by then, but we cannot know that until we see savings, library income and our actual expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep earning at West Yard, save from full months and ask the steward for a yearly safety report on site machines. In 2032 I'd take paid fitting shifts if there are any and try the proven digital checks Ivo uses; before 2034 we'd calculate whether I could reduce hours or need to apply to another builder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel watchful but less pressed than in the fast case. A few extra years could turn our savings into a real choice, though I will not promise retirement before doing the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a yearly safety report include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Near misses, repair delays and who stopped a machine when it behaved badly. Workers need the ordinary details, not just a claim that accidents are down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to leave construction at sixty-six?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might, if our figures allow it and my body has had enough. I could also keep doing paid lighter fitting; there is no signed retirement date in our house.

say: I'd ask for a **fault record** before new machines spread.
I'd bargain for a **real training schedule** during the five-year lead-in.
think: At **sixty-six**, robots could reduce fitting shifts.
I might work less only if **household figures** support that choice.
do: Keep **West Yard wages** and save after full months.
Request a **yearly safety report** through the steward.
Take paid **fitting work** in 2032 and test Ivo's proven digital checks.
feel: **Watchful**, with more time to build a choice and check the numbers.
S3.quote: I could also keep doing paid lighter fitting; there is no signed retirement date in our house.
fieldNote: He converts the five-year window into **specific safety reporting** and continued paid work.
Retirement remains conditional on **measured expenses** and savings, despite a strong current cushion.

steps.text: Save extra after full paid site months
Request annual machine safety reports through the steward
Keep taking paid fitting shifts in 2032
Try Ivo’s proven digital checks during paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade should be enough time to write fair site rules before robots begin working beside people. I would still demand that workers see the test results themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when robots can handle site tasks. Priya and I might have stopped full-time work by then, but I may still want paid light fitting if our savings and her wages are short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking site shifts and saving from full months while the pay is good. In 2037 I'd take suitable paid repair work if needed and ask the branch to review the safety rules for AI-generated drawings; before 2039 Priya and I would count our income before I give up the last shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly calm about the distant machine dates. My work today is well paid, there are other builders nearby and we have time to make our finances clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children be part of that income calculation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our children are making their own way and their wages belong to their homes. They can visit us without being asked to fund us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could make you change jobs sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A site with repeated unsafe shortcuts would send me to another builder while there are plenty of openings. I won't stay merely to preserve a familiar route.

say: I'd demand **visible test results** and fair rules before site robots spread.
I'd use the **decade** to keep worker voices in safety decisions.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still want paid fitting after thinking AI arrives.
At **seventy-one**, whether I stop depends on savings and Priya's wages.
do: Keep **site shifts** and save from full paid months.
Take **light repair work** in 2037 if income is needed.
Review **safety rules** through the branch before robots spread.
feel: Fairly **calm** because pay, savings and local openings offer time.
S4.quote: A site with repeated unsafe shortcuts would send me to another builder while there are plenty of openings.
fieldNote: The long horizon and **strong cushion** ease Zane's income concern, though he keeps paid work conditional on real need.
He treats **unsafe shortcuts** as a reason to change builders and grown children's wages as outside his retirement plan.

steps.text: Keep taking paid site work while fit
Save extra after full paid months
Ask the union branch to review AI drawing safety

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because a robot might reach door work by the time I'm sixty-three, before Priya and I know whether our savings can carry us. Paid safety training, proper notice and real housing-maintenance vacancies would let me choose while I still have wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether the person checking a machine's work is given time to do it. A safety check squeezed into an unpaid break is no check at all.

headlineQuote: A safety check squeezed into an unpaid break is no check at all.
portrait: Zane is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** carpenter who entered site work after years as a caretaker.
Higher site pay, Priya's library job and **ten months saved** give him room to evaluate changes.
He uses AI occasionally and adopts tools after **real delivery tests**.
He seeks paid training and **safety records** through the union while keeping retirement tied to actual finances.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could reach his hands-on door work by 2031, before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid safety training**, notice and real housing-maintenance vacancies.
